title: Be more strategic
author: Nick Hart
summary: Opening a series on leadership work in schools, Nick Hart takes aim at one of the most common and least defined pieces of advice given to school leaders: 'be more strategic'. He argues that the ambiguity is costly, because when strategic work is poorly defined roles blur, workload escalates, senior leaders are pulled into operational detail and middle leaders are stretched between delivery and direction. Drawing on Elliott Jaques's levels of work, he distinguishes execution, coordination and direction-shaping by the complexity of judgement and time horizon each demands. He rejects the equation of strategy with long-term planning, defining strategic work instead by what a leader is accountable for holding in view, such as the organisation's relationship to its environment and which problems matter. He then explains why schools are especially vulnerable to role confusion: moral purpose that makes every intervention feel urgent, highly visible operational problems, and weak shared language for different kinds of leadership work. Hart frames these as organisational design problems rather than individual failings, and ends by asking how schools can be designed so strategic work can actually happen.

Using Jaques's levels of work, he separates execution, coordination and direction-shaping by the complexity of judgement and the time horizon over which decisions carry consequences.

Strategic work is defined not by planning further ahead but by what a leader holds in view: the organisation's relationship to its environment, reconciling ambiguity, and choosing which problems matter.
Moral purpose makes schools uniquely prone to role collapse, as leaders step in 'just this once' to help and the exception becomes the norm.
quotes: In schools, the ambiguity matters. When being strategic is poorly defined, roles blur and workload quietly escalates. Senior leaders feel pulled into operational detail.
Over time, this not only exhausts people but distorts the organisation because different kinds of leadership work are confused, collapsed or misallocated.

Jaques was not writing about schools but about organisations more generally. His central insight was that work differs in the complexity of judgement it requires and the time horizon over which decisions carry real consequences.

One common misunderstanding is to equate strategic leadership with long term planning. Planning matters, of course but in Jaques’ terms, planning is not what distinguishes strategic work. Strategic work is defined by what you are accountable for holding in view at the same time.

The work feels urgent because it matters. Leaders step in just this once to help, fix, or protect and the exception becomes the norm. Teachers are busy and it feels like an act of service to help in the moment, in every moment.
Timetables break, staff are absent, parents complain, lessons happen every hour. Strategic work is quieter and easier to crowd out. We’ll do it when the students have gone home or at the weekend.

If we want schools that are adaptive rather than reactive, coherent rather than fragmented, and humane rather than exhausted, we need to be more precise about the work we are asking leaders to do and how we protect it. The next question, then, is not simply whether leaders understand what being strategic means but how we design our schools to enable strategic work to actually happen.
